title: Decisions, Control and the Social Brain
summary: How prefrontal and parietal circuits weigh evidence, compute value, control behavior and model other minds.

lessons.title: Executive Control: Inhibition, Switching and Conflict Monitoring

levels.kid:
Imagine you're playing "Simon Says." The leader shouts "Touch your nose!" but didn't say "Simon says." Your hand wants to move, but you stop it. That stopping power is called **inhibition**.

Your brain has a boss team at the front of your head, behind your forehead. Scientists call its skills **executive control**. The boss team helps you:
- Stop doing something you shouldn't do
- Switch from one game's rules to another
- Notice when you're about to make a mistake

There's even a little brain helper that acts like a smoke alarm. When two choices fight each other, it beeps inside your head. Then you slow down and think more carefully. This boss team keeps growing until you are grown up.
levels.hs:
**Executive control** (also called executive function or cognitive control) is the set of brain processes that let you guide behavior by goals instead of habits. Psychologist Akira Miyake described three core parts:
- **Inhibition**: stopping a strong, automatic response.
- **Switching** (shifting): flexibly changing between tasks or rules.
- **Updating**: refreshing what you hold in working memory.

A classic example is the **Stroop task**. You see the word RED printed in blue ink and must name the ink color. Reading is automatic, so the word interferes. People are slower and make more errors on these "incongruent" trials. That slowdown is the **Stroop effect**, and it shows conflict between two responses.

Much of this control depends on the **prefrontal cortex (PFC)**, the front part of the frontal lobe. A region on the brain's middle surface, the **anterior cingulate cortex (ACC)**, seems to detect conflict, like an alarm noticing that two responses are competing. The lateral PFC then boosts attention to the task-relevant information.

The PFC is one of the last brain areas to fully mature, continuing into the mid-20s. That helps explain why impulse control keeps improving through the teen years. Damage to the PFC, as in the famous case of Phineas Gage, can make people impulsive or rigid.
levels.college:
Executive control lets goals override habits. Miyake and colleagues (2000) used latent-variable analysis and found three related but separable components: **inhibition**, **shifting** and **updating**. They share a common factor.

**Inhibition.** In the **stop-signal task**, people respond to a go cue but must cancel the response when a stop signal follows. The **stop-signal reaction time (SSRT)** estimates how fast stopping happens, typically around 200-250 ms in healthy adults. Key nodes:
- **Right inferior frontal gyrus (rIFG)**
- **Pre-supplementary motor area (pre-SMA)**
- **Subthalamic nucleus (STN)** of the basal ganglia

The **hyperdirect pathway** runs from cortex straight to the STN. It can rapidly brake motor output by exciting the inhibitory output nuclei, the globus pallidus internus and the substantia nigra pars reticulata.

**Switching.** In task-switching paradigms, responses are slower right after a rule change. This **switch cost** persists partly even with time to prepare, a remainder called the residual cost. Switching engages the dorsolateral PFC (dlPFC), the inferior frontal junction and the posterior parietal cortex.

**Conflict monitoring.** Botvinick and colleagues (2001) proposed that the **dorsal ACC** detects conflict between competing responses and signals the dlPFC to raise control. Evidence includes:
- The **conflict adaptation (Gratton) effect**: interference is smaller after an incongruent trial.
- **Post-error slowing.**
- The **error-related negativity (ERN)**, an EEG deflection about 50-100 ms after an error, generated near the ACC.

**Neurochemistry.** Prefrontal **dopamine** (via D1 receptors) and **norepinephrine** (via α2A receptors) tune PFC working memory along an inverted-U curve: too little or too much impairs performance. Methylphenidate and atomoxetine act partly through these catecholamines, which helps explain their use in ADHD.
levels.phd:
Computationally, executive control is often framed as **biased competition**. Miller and Cohen's (2001) integrative theory proposes that lateral PFC actively maintains goal representations, often called task sets. These send top-down bias signals that favor weaker, task-relevant pathways over prepotent ones. In the Stroop connectionist model by Cohen, Dunbar and McClelland (1990), a "color-naming" task unit adds activation to color pathways. Interference emerges because the word pathway has stronger connection weights, built up through practice.

The **conflict-monitoring theory** (Botvinick et al., 2001) formalized conflict as Hopfield energy: the product of co-active, mutually incompatible response units. Conflict detected by the dorsal ACC adjusts control on the next trial. This explains conflict adaptation. A confound soon emerged, however: in two-choice Stroop designs, congruent-after-congruent trials repeat stimuli. When feature-integration and contingency-learning confounds are removed, the Gratton effect shrinks but survives in many studies.

ACC theory has since broadened:
- **PRO model** (Alexander and Brown, 2011): the medial PFC signals the difference between predicted and actual outcomes. Conflict is one case of this.
- **Expected value of control (EVC)** (Shenhav, Botvinick and Cohen, 2013): the dACC estimates whether investing control is worth its intrinsic cost. This links control to effort and motivation.

For inhibition, the **horse-race model** (Logan and Cowan, 1984) treats go and stop processes as independent racers. SSRT is inferred from the inhibition function. Primate frontal eye field and superior colliculus recordings (Hanes and Schall) found movement neurons whose activity was halted just before SSRT, consistent with a neural race. Aron's rIFG-pre-SMA-STN model is supported by human STN recordings and lesion data. Critics such as Hampshire argue the rIFG reflects detecting important cues rather than a dedicated brake. Recent work suggests stopping proceeds in two stages: a fast, nonselective pause, then a slower cancellation (Schmidt and Berke; the pause-then-cancel model).

For switching, the residual switch cost is attributed to **task-set inertia** (Allport): lingering activation of the previous task set. Backward inhibition (Mayr and Keele) shows the old set is actively suppressed.
levels.expert:
Clinically and translationally, executive control is where cognitive neuroscience meets neurosurgery and psychiatry.

**Deep brain stimulation (DBS).** STN DBS for Parkinson's disease improves motor symptoms. Frank and colleagues (2007), however, showed it can impair the conflict-induced slowing that normally holds back hasty choices. Patients made impulsive selections when options had similar value, and medial frontal theta no longer predicted slowing. Clinically, impulsivity and, rarely, mood changes after STN targeting inform patient selection and contact programming. Dopaminergic therapy has its own risk: **impulse control disorders**, linked especially to D2/D3 agonists, occur in a substantial minority of Parkinson's patients.

**Resection planning.** Lesions of the dorsal ACC and medial frontal cortex can produce apathy, akinetic mutism (with bilateral damage) or reduced error awareness. Resection of the supplementary motor area causes a usually transient **SMA syndrome**. Surgeons counsel patients about it and map the area with awake or electrocorticographic methods. Dominant inferior frontal resections risk language deficits, so mapping inhibitory function in the right IFG is an emerging intraoperative goal.

**Biomarkers.** The ERN is enlarged in obsessive-compulsive disorder and anxiety, and blunted in some externalizing conditions. It is a candidate transdiagnostic marker in the NIMH RDoC framework, although test-retest reliability is good while diagnostic specificity remains modest. **Frontal midline theta** (4-8 Hz), likely generated in the medial PFC, tracks the need for control. Theta coupling with lateral PFC offers a mechanism for implementing control and a target for closed-loop stimulation.

**Methodological pitfalls.**
- SSRT estimates become biased when participants slow strategically or when go processes violate the race model's independence assumption. Consensus guidelines (Verbruggen et al., 2019) recommend the integration method with replacement of go omissions.
- Executive tasks show the **reliability paradox**: robust group effects but poor test-retest reliability of individual differences, which weakens correlational and clinical studies.
- "Ego depletion" claims failed large preregistered replications. The EVC framework recasts fatigue as a shifting cost-benefit calculation, not a depleted resource.

**Open questions.** Is "inhibition" a unitary process, or emergent from competition? Does the dACC compute conflict, surprise or control value? How do neuromodulators set control intensity, as in the adaptive gain theory of locus coeruleus norepinephrine (Aston-Jones and Cohen)?

Stopping uses the rIFG, pre-SMA and STN via the hyperdirect pathway
Task switching produces switch costs, including a residual cost
The dorsal ACC monitors conflict; the ERN follows errors
Prefrontal dopamine and norepinephrine tune control on an inverted-U curve

advancedTest.explain: This is the reliability paradox. Tasks that make an effect consistent across people leave little stable variance between individuals, which harms correlational studies.

lessons.title: Value-Based Choice: Orbitofrontal and Ventromedial Prefrontal Cortex

levels.kid:
Imagine you can pick one treat: an apple or a cookie. How does your brain choose? It gives each treat a secret score, like points in a game. Then it picks the one with more points.

The score changes with how you feel. If you just ate three cookies, a cookie gets fewer points, and the apple might win!

The part of the brain that keeps these scores sits right behind your eyes. Scientists call it the **orbitofrontal cortex**. "Orbit" means the eye socket.

Long ago, a man named Phineas Gage hurt the front of his brain in an accident. Afterward, he made poor choices. That helped scientists learn that the front of the brain helps us choose well.
levels.hs:
Every day you make **value-based choices**: decisions where no answer is objectively right, only better or worse for you, like pizza versus sushi. Neuroscientists study how the brain assigns **subjective value**, meaning how much something is worth to you right now.

Two neighboring regions at the bottom-front of the brain are central:
- The **orbitofrontal cortex (OFC)**, sitting just above the eye sockets (orbits).
- The **ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC)**, along the lower middle surface of the frontal lobes.

These areas take information about options (taste, price, delay, effort) and turn it into a kind of common currency, so very different things can be compared.

A key experiment: researchers recorded single neurons in monkey OFC while the monkeys chose between different amounts of juice flavors. Some neurons fired in proportion to how much the monkey valued an option, not to its color or size. Value depends on state: if you have just eaten chocolate until you're full, OFC responses to chocolate drop. This is called **devaluation**.

Damage matters too. Phineas Gage (1848) survived an iron rod through his frontal lobe and became impulsive. Modern patients with vmPFC damage, like "Elliot," studied by Antonio Damasio, kept normal IQ but made disastrous real-life decisions. This shows that choosing well needs more than intelligence: it needs a working value system.
levels.college:
Value-based (economic) choice is usually split into stages: represent the options, assign each a **subjective value**, compare values, act, then learn from the outcome. OFC and vmPFC are most tied to the valuation and comparison stages.

**Anatomy.** OFC is the ventral surface of the frontal lobe. It receives converging input from every sensory modality (taste, smell, vision, visceral signals) plus the amygdala, hippocampus and midbrain dopamine neurons. vmPFC is the adjacent medial wall, including ventral area 32, 10m and 14. It is strongly linked to ventral striatum and the default mode network.

**Key findings.**
- **Padoa-Schioppa and Assad (2006)**: monkey OFC neurons encode "offer value" (value of one option), "chosen value" (value of whatever is picked), and "taste" (identity of the chosen good). These are the ingredients of a decision.
- **Common currency**: human fMRI shows vmPFC BOLD scales with willingness-to-pay across foods, trinkets and money (Plassmann, O'Doherty and Rangel, 2007; Chib et al., 2009).
- **Sensory-specific satiety**: eating one food to satiety lowers OFC responses to that food but not to others (Rolls; O'Doherty et al., 2000).
- **Reversal learning**: OFC lesions in monkeys and rodents impair switching when stimulus-reward contingencies flip, causing perseveration.

**Lesion evidence.** vmPFC patients perform poorly on the **Iowa Gambling Task**, continuing to choose decks with big rewards but bigger losses. Damasio's **somatic marker hypothesis** proposed they lack bodily "gut feelings" that bias choice. vmPFC damage also produces inconsistent, intransitive preferences (choosing A over B, B over C, yet C over A) (Fellows and Farah, 2007).

**Modulators.** Value integrates delay (temporal discounting), effort, risk and social context. vmPFC activity also tracks goal value and is shaped by self-control signals from dorsolateral PFC (Hare et al., 2009).
levels.phd:
Valuation work has converged on several computational ideas, each with live disputes.

**Good-based model.** Padoa-Schioppa argues choice occurs in the space of goods, inside OFC, before action planning. OFC offer-value cells show **range adaptation**: their firing rates rescale to the range of values on offer in a block, maximizing coding efficiency. Microstimulation and inactivation studies (Ballesta et al., 2020) show biasing OFC activity shifts choices, supporting a causal role. The alternative, action-based models, places comparison in parietal and premotor circuits.

**Normalization.** Louie, Glimcher and colleagues showed value signals are divisively normalized by the summed value of the choice set, which predicts context effects such as the decline in choice accuracy when a third, irrelevant option is added. This links valuation to canonical cortical computation.

**OFC as a cognitive map.** Wilson, Takahashi, Schoenbaum and Niv (2014) proposed OFC represents the current **task state**, especially states not directly observable. Under this view, reversal deficits reflect failure to infer a hidden state change rather than failed value updating. Supporting evidence: OFC is needed when outcome identity, not just magnitude, matters (devaluation, sensory preconditioning, Pavlovian-to-instrumental specificity), while purely cached values survive OFC loss.

**Reappraising reversal.** Rudebeck, Murray and colleagues found that excitotoxic OFC lesions in macaques, which spare passing fibers, did not impair object reversal learning, unlike older aspiration lesions. This reattributed classic reversal deficits partly to damaged white matter, though devaluation deficits persisted. It is a notable lesson in lesion methodology.

**vmPFC dynamics.** Hunt, Behrens and colleagues used MEG plus a biophysical attractor model to show vmPFC signals evolve from summed value to value difference during a choice, consistent with competition by mutual inhibition. Strait and colleagues found similar sequential comparison in single vmPFC neurons.

**Subdivisions.** Medial OFC/vmPFC appears to encode value for comparison; lateral OFC handles credit assignment, linking specific outcomes to the choices that caused them (Walton et al., 2010). Rodent-primate homology remains contested, since rodents lack granular prefrontal cortex.
levels.expert:
The clinical and translational face of valuation circuits differs sharply from the tidy single-neuron picture.

**Clinical syndromes.** Ventral frontal damage from anterior communicating artery aneurysm rupture, traumatic contusion (the orbital surface striking the anterior cranial fossa), or **olfactory groove and planum meningiomas** produces apathy, disinhibition, poor social judgment and impulsive spending, often with preserved neuropsychological scores. Standard bedside tests (MMSE, even Wisconsin Card Sorting) can miss it. This is the "frontal paradox": devastating real-world dysfunction with normal testing. Collateral history from family is often more informative than formal scores. In behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia, early orbitofrontal and anterior insular atrophy drive overeating, sweet preference and financial exploitation vulnerability.

**Neurosurgical relevance.** Subfrontal approaches, frontal lobectomy and gyrus rectus resection risk ventral value circuits. Postoperative personality change is often reported by relatives before it appears in clinic. Preserving vmPFC and ventral striatal connections (uncinate fasciculus, anterior limb of internal capsule) is part of planning.

**Psychiatry.** Hyperactive OFC-striatal loops are implicated in obsessive-compulsive disorder. Ahmari et al. (2013) showed repeated optogenetic stimulation of OFC-to-ventromedial-striatum projections in mice produced persistent grooming, while Burguière et al. (2013) found that stimulating lateral OFC suppressed it. Deep brain stimulation targets the ventral capsule/ventral striatum for refractory OCD and is being studied in depression, where subgenual cingulate overlaps vmPFC. In addiction, OFC encodes inflated drug-associated value and impaired devaluation sensitivity.

**Pitfalls.** vmPFC BOLD tracks value but also arousal, salience, self-relevance and default mode activity, so "value signal" claims need careful designs controlling attention. The orbital surface also suffers from fMRI susceptibility artifact near the sinuses, causing signal dropout; multiband sequences and tilted slices help. Human lesion groups are typically small and heterogeneous.

**Open questions.** Is choice computed in goods space or distributed across action circuits? Does OFC store value or a state map from which value is derived? How do serotonin and dopamine inputs tune range adaptation and patience? Closed-loop stimulation and large-scale recordings in patients undergoing intracranial monitoring are now addressing these directly.

keyPoints: Value-based choice compares options by their subjective value to you

OFC neurons encode offer value, chosen value and chosen identity
Value drops with satiety (devaluation), and OFC responses track this
vmPFC damage impairs real-life decisions despite normal IQ
OFC may represent hidden task states, not just stored value

Removing the need for dopamine inputs to learn

advancedTest.q: Under the 'cognitive map' view, why would OFC lesions impair reversal learning?
choices: The animal fails to infer a hidden change in task state
Motor output to the chosen target is blocked
Reward signals from dopamine neurons are abolished
Visual cues can no longer be perceived
advancedTest.explain: Wilson and colleagues proposed OFC represents unobservable task states; reversal deficits reflect failed state inference, not lost value per se.

advancedTest.q: Divisive normalization predicts what happens when a third, low-value option is added to a two-option choice?
choices: The added option is filtered out by value neurons
The best option's coded value rises sharply
Value signals become independent of the choice set
Choice accuracy between the top two options can decline
advancedTest.explain: Normalization divides each value by the summed set value, compressing differences between the top options and reducing accuracy.

lessons.title: Evidence Accumulation and the Drift-Diffusion Model

levels.kid:
Imagine you are deciding if a cloudy sky means rain. Each dark cloud is a little clue for "rain." Each patch of sun is a clue for "no rain." You keep adding up the clues in your head.

When enough clues pile up on one side, you decide! Maybe you grab your umbrella.

Your brain does this all the time. Some brain cells act like a jar filling up with marbles. Each clue drops in a marble. When the jar reaches the top line, you choose.

If the clues are clear, the jar fills fast and you decide quickly. If the clues are mixed up, it fills slowly. You can also set the line lower to be fast, but then you make more mistakes.
levels.hs:
Many decisions are not instant. Your brain gathers **evidence** over time and commits once it has enough. Scientists call this **evidence accumulation**.

The most famous description is the **drift-diffusion model (DDM)**. Picture a dot moving between two lines, one for each choice:
- The dot starts in the middle.
- Each moment, new evidence nudges it toward one line. The average push is the **drift rate**. Clear evidence means a high drift rate.
- The evidence is noisy, so the dot wobbles randomly. That wobble is the "diffusion."
- When the dot touches a line, called the **decision boundary** or threshold, you choose that option.

The model explains the **speed-accuracy tradeoff**. Wide boundaries give slow but accurate decisions. Narrow boundaries give fast but error-prone ones. Imagine a goalkeeper facing a penalty kick. Waiting longer gathers more evidence about the kick's direction, but waiting too long means missing the ball.

A real example comes from monkey experiments. Monkeys watched a cloud of moving dots and decided whether most dots moved left or right. Neurons in a brain area called **LIP** (in the parietal lobe) increased their firing gradually, faster when the motion was clearer. A choice was made when the firing reached a fixed level, just like the dot hitting the line.
levels.college:
Sequential sampling models treat a two-choice decision as the integration of noisy evidence until a bound is reached. The **drift-diffusion model** (Ratcliff, 1978) is the standard version. Its core parameters are:
- **Drift rate (v)**: mean rate of evidence accumulation. It reflects stimulus strength and the quality of processing.
- **Boundary separation (a)**: distance between the two bounds. It sets response caution.
- **Starting point (z)**: a bias toward one option. Prior probability or reward asymmetry can shift it.
- **Non-decision time (Ter)**: time for sensory encoding and motor execution, outside the decision itself.

The model fits more than mean reaction time (RT). It predicts full **RT distributions**, which are right-skewed, and accuracy together. It can also explain why errors are sometimes slower or faster than correct responses. Adding trial-to-trial variability in drift or starting point captures these patterns.

**Neural correlates.** In the random-dot motion task, area **MT** neurons encode momentary motion. **LIP** neurons ramp up their firing in a way that resembles the integral of that evidence. Roitman and Shadlen (2002) found that LIP ramps steepened with motion coherence and converged on a common level about 70 ms before the saccade, consistent with a threshold. Similar buildup occurs in the **frontal eye fields** and the **superior colliculus**.

**Speed-accuracy tradeoff.** When people are told to hurry, model fits mainly show reduced boundary separation. Imaging links speed emphasis to increased baseline activity in the **pre-SMA** and **striatum**. One proposal is that the basal ganglia release a response once cortical accumulators reach a bound.

**Why it matters.** The DDM breaks behavior into separate processes. Two groups can have the same mean RT for different reasons: lower drift (poorer evidence quality) or wider bounds (more caution). This makes the model useful in aging, psychiatry and drug studies.
levels.phd:
The DDM is the continuous limit of the **sequential probability ratio test** (Wald; Wald and Wolfowitz). Accumulating the log-likelihood ratio to fixed bounds minimizes expected sample size for a given error rate. This optimality, stated for fixed-duration-cost settings by Bogacz et al. (2006), motivates the model normatively. Reward rate is maximized at a boundary that depends on drift, noise and intertrial intervals.

Formally, dx = v dt + s dW, with absorbing bounds at 0 and a. First-passage-time distributions have closed-form series solutions. Fitting is done by maximum likelihood, χ² on quantiles, or hierarchical Bayesian methods (HDDM; Wiecki et al., 2013). The full Ratcliff model adds variability in drift (η), starting point (sz) and non-decision time (st). Drift variability produces slow errors, and starting-point variability produces fast errors.

Related models differ in architecture:
- **Race and LBA models** use independent accumulators per option, which generalizes naturally to many alternatives.
- **Leaky competing accumulators** (Usher and McClelland, 2001) add leak and mutual inhibition.
- **Attractor networks** (Wang, 2002) implement integration through slow NMDA-mediated recurrent excitation and pooled inhibition. This is a biophysical mechanism for ramping and winner-take-all dynamics.

The **collapsing bound or urgency** debate concerns whether bounds narrow over time. Churchland et al. (2008) reported an urgency signal in LIP that grew with elapsed time. Behavioral evidence for collapsing bounds is mixed across paradigms.

A major controversy concerns **causality and the ramp**. Latimer et al. (2015) argued that single-trial LIP dynamics may look more like discrete **steps** than continuous ramps, with averaging creating the appearance of ramps. Later population recordings with Neuropixels supported ramp-like integration in many trials, so the debate continues. Katz et al. (2016) found that muscimol inactivation of LIP barely affected motion decisions. Integration may therefore be distributed, with LIP reflecting rather than computing it. Rodent work places the integrators in FOF and PPC, with dissociable roles.

The DDM also extends to value: the **attentional DDM** (Krajbich et al., 2010) biases drift toward the item being fixated.
levels.expert:
Clinically and in research, the DDM serves mainly as a **measurement model**. It separates latent processes that ordinary RT and accuracy confound. Some practical points:

- **Parameter recovery first.** With fewer than roughly 100 trials per condition, the variability parameters are poorly identified, and drift and boundary trade off. Simplified fits such as EZ-diffusion or hierarchical pooling are more robust in patient samples. Always simulate from fitted values to check that the model reproduces the RT quantiles.
- **Contaminants.** Fast guesses and lapses distort fits. Use mixture components or RT cutoffs, and report how outliers were handled.
- **Selective influence is assumed, not guaranteed.** Speed instructions can change drift as well as boundary. Test this rather than fixing parameters by assumption.

**Psychiatry and neurology.** In ADHD, the most replicated finding is lower drift rate, linked to elevated RT variability, rather than impulsive low boundaries. In Parkinson's disease, deep brain stimulation of the **subthalamic nucleus** reduces the boundary increase normally seen under high conflict, producing hasty choices. Frank and Cavanagh linked this to medial frontal theta raising the threshold via the STN. This gives a mechanistic explanation for impulsivity after DBS that matters for surgical candidates and their counseling. Dopaminergic medication changes boundary and starting-point bias in ways related to reward sensitivity. Stimulant effects in healthy and ADHD groups are often captured as increased drift.

**Human electrophysiology.** The **centroparietal positivity** (CPP; O'Connell, Kelly and colleagues, 2012) is an EEG signal that builds to a threshold independent of sensory modality. It behaves like a domain-general accumulator, and its buildup rate predicts RT. It is a noninvasive biomarker of how evidence accumulates.

**Open questions.**
- Do bounds collapse in natural settings, and is urgency a neuromodulatory signal, possibly noradrenergic gain?
- How is integration distributed across cortex, basal ganglia and colliculus, given that inactivating any single node seldom abolishes it?
- How do confidence and changes of mind arise? Post-decision accumulation (Resulaj et al., 2009) suggests that integration continues after commitment.
- Can DDM parameters serve as validated computational-psychiatry endpoints in trials? Test-retest reliability is moderate for drift and weaker for other parameters.

keyPoints: Decisions often arise by accumulating noisy evidence until a threshold is reached
DDM parameters: drift rate, boundary separation, starting point, non-decision time
Wider boundaries give slower but more accurate choices (speed-accuracy tradeoff)
LIP neurons ramp with evidence strength in the random-dot motion task
The DDM implements the optimal sequential probability ratio test
Debates: ramps vs steps, collapsing bounds, and whether LIP is causal

test.q: In the drift-diffusion model, the drift rate reflects:
choices: The prior bias toward one of the options
The distance between the two decision bounds
The average rate at which evidence accumulates
The time needed to press the response button
test.explain: Drift rate is the mean push of evidence per unit time. It is higher when stimuli are clearer.

test.q: Widening the boundary separation in the DDM mainly produces:
choices: A shift in bias toward one option
test.explain: Wider bounds require more evidence, so responses are more cautious: slower but more accurate.

test.q: In Roitman and Shadlen's random-dot task, LIP neurons:
choices: Fired at a fixed rate whatever the coherence
Encoded the color rather than the motion
Stopped firing once the stimulus appeared
Ramped faster when motion coherence was higher
test.explain: LIP activity built up more steeply with stronger motion and converged on a common level before the saccade.

test.q: Which area encodes the momentary motion evidence that LIP appears to integrate?
choices: Area V1 in the occipital pole
test.explain: MT neurons signal moment-to-moment motion direction. LIP activity resembles the integral of that signal.

test.q: A starting point shifted toward one bound most likely reflects:
choices: Prior expectation or a reward asymmetry
Poor quality of the sensory evidence
Slower motor output on each trial
test.explain: Starting point encodes bias from priors or unequal rewards. Caution is set by boundary separation.

test.q: The non-decision time parameter covers:
choices: How far apart the decision bounds are
The noise added to evidence on each trial
test.explain: Ter captures processes outside the decision itself, such as encoding and movement.

test.q: Two groups have the same mean RT. Why might the DDM still separate them?
choices: It assumes the groups share identical parameters
Lower drift or wider bounds give the same mean RT
It measures RT more precisely than a stopwatch does
It ignores accuracy and relies on mean RT alone
test.explain: By fitting RT distributions together with accuracy, the DDM can tell poorer evidence quality apart from greater caution.

test.q: Reaction time distributions in choice tasks are typically:
test.explain: RT distributions have a long slow tail. The DDM predicts this right skew naturally.

test.q: Emphasizing speed over accuracy has been linked to increased baseline activity in:
test.explain: Imaging links speed emphasis to higher baseline activity in pre-SMA and striatum, which brings activity closer to threshold.

test.q: The dot in the model wobbles randomly because the evidence contains ___.
test.explain: Noisy evidence makes the decision variable wobble randomly around its average drift; this is the diffusion part of the model.

test.q: Which parietal area (three-letter abbreviation) shows ramping activity during motion decisions in monkeys?
test.explain: The lateral intraparietal area shows evidence-dependent buildup toward a threshold.

test.q: The DDM explains the speed-___ tradeoff through the setting of its boundaries.
test.explain: Narrow bounds favor speed and wide bounds favor accuracy.

kidTest.q: What does your brain add up before deciding?
kidTest.explain: The brain piles up clues until there are enough to choose.

kidTest.q: When clues are very clear, you usually decide:
kidTest.explain: Clear clues fill the jar fast, so you decide quickly.

kidTest.q: What happens if you set the line lower to decide fast?
kidTest.explain: Deciding with fewer clues is faster but leads to more mistakes.

kidTest.q: In the lesson, each clue is like dropping in a:
kidTest.explain: Brain cells act like a jar filling with marbles, one for each clue.

kidTest.q: When the jar reaches the top line, you make a c _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Reaching the line means you have enough clues to choose.

advancedTest.q: Adding trial-to-trial drift variability to the DDM mainly lets it explain:
choices: Errors that are slower than correct responses
A constant non-decision time across subjects
Errors that are faster than correct responses
advancedTest.explain: Drift variability makes errors come mostly from low-drift trials, which are slow. Starting-point variability produces fast errors instead.

advancedTest.q: Katz et al. found that LIP inactivation barely affected motion decisions. The best inference is that:
choices: Integration may be distributed, with LIP reflecting it
Drift-diffusion models fail to describe monkey choices
The MT area integrates motion and also makes the final choice
Monkeys in that task do not integrate evidence over time
advancedTest.explain: Ramps can correlate with a computation without being needed for it. The result points to distributed or redundant integration.

advancedTest.q: After STN deep brain stimulation, a Parkinson's patient makes hasty choices under high conflict. In DDM terms this is best described as:
choices: A lower drift rate whenever both options conflict
A failure to raise the boundary under conflict
A starting point shifted toward the worse option
A longer non-decision time for each response
advancedTest.explain: Medial frontal theta normally raises the threshold through the STN under conflict. DBS disrupts this adjustment.

advancedTest.q: Latimer et al. argued that averaged LIP ramps could be misleading because:
choices: Averaging removes any link between firing and choice
Single trials may hold discrete steps at varied times
LIP neurons respond to stimulus color rather than motion
Ramps appear mainly when no motion stimulus is present
advancedTest.explain: Averaging steps that occur at different times on each trial produces a smooth ramp, so the average alone cannot tell the two apart.

lessons.title: Model-Based vs Model-Free Learning

levels.kid:
Imagine you walk to school every day. After a while, your feet just go the same way without thinking. That is a **habit**. Your brain remembers "this worked before, do it again."

Now imagine the usual road is closed. You stop and picture a map in your head. You think, "If I turn left at the park, I can still get there." That is **planning**.

Scientists call the habit way **model-free** and the map way **model-based**. Habits are fast and easy, but they can be wrong when things change. Planning is slower and takes more effort, but it helps when the world surprises you.

Your brain uses both, and it picks the best one for each moment.
levels.hs:
Your brain can learn which actions are good in two different ways.

**Model-free learning** stores how good an action has been in the past, with no picture of *why*. It runs on **prediction errors**: the difference between what you expected and what you got. If a result is better than expected, the action gets a bit more value. The chemical messenger **dopamine** signals these errors. Model-free learning is fast to use but slow to update, and it is the basis of **habits**.

**Model-based learning** builds an internal **model**, a mental map of how actions lead to situations and what each situation is worth. To choose, you mentally simulate the future. This is flexible but takes time and working memory.

A classic test is **outcome devaluation**. Rats learn to press a lever for food. Then the food is made unappealing, for example by letting them eat it until they are full. A rat using a model-based (goal-directed) strategy stops pressing, because it knows the lever leads to food it no longer wants. A rat with heavy overtraining keeps pressing out of habit.

The **prefrontal cortex** and the front part of the striatum support goal-directed control. A rear-and-side part of the striatum supports habits. Healthy behavior means switching wisely between the two.
levels.college:
The model-based (MB) and model-free (MF) distinction comes from **reinforcement learning (RL)** in computer science and maps onto the psychological contrast between **goal-directed actions** and **habits**.

**Model-free RL** caches action values. In **temporal-difference (TD) learning**, the prediction error is δ = r + γV(s') − V(s), where r is the reward and γ discounts future value. Values are nudged by a learning rate α times δ. Phasic firing of midbrain **dopamine neurons** (VTA and substantia nigra) matches δ. They fire bursts to unexpected rewards, shift their response to predictive cues, and dip when an expected reward is omitted.

**Model-based RL** learns a **transition model** (which state follows each action) and a **reward model**. It computes values on demand by searching forward through possible futures.

Trade-offs:
- MF: cheap to use, but **inflexible**. When outcomes change, it has to relearn through new experience.
- MB: flexible, adapts at once to devaluation or new routes, but costly and limited by working memory.

Neural substrates (from rodent lesion work by Balleine, Dickinson and colleagues):
- Goal-directed control: prelimbic cortex and **dorsomedial striatum** (in primates, the caudate and the ventromedial and orbitofrontal PFC).
- Habits: infralimbic cortex and **dorsolateral striatum** (in primates, the putamen).

Evidence comes from two sources:
- **Outcome devaluation**: goal-directed animals reduce responding after the reward is devalued, while habitual ones do not.
- **Contingency degradation**: here reward is delivered regardless of the action, which also separates the two systems.

Overtraining and interval reinforcement schedules push behavior toward habit.

In humans, the **two-step task** (Daw et al., 2011) separates the two strategies. A first choice leads, usually (70%) or rarely (30%), to one of two second-stage states with drifting reward probabilities. After a rare transition that is rewarded, an MF learner repeats its first choice. An MB learner switches, because it knows the other option more reliably reaches that rewarding state. People show a mixture of both patterns.
levels.phd:
Daw, Niv and Dayan (2005) proposed that the brain runs MB and MF controllers in parallel and arbitrates by **relative uncertainty**. MB estimates are accurate early but noisy because of computational limits. MF estimates become reliable with extensive experience. This explains why overtraining yields habits. Later work (Lee, Shimojo and O'Doherty, 2014) found that **ventrolateral PFC and frontopolar cortex** track the reliability of each system and modulate their influence. Other models frame arbitration as **cost-benefit**: MB control is recruited when its reward advantage exceeds the cost of cognitive effort (Kool, Gershman and Cushman).

In the two-step task, ventral striatal BOLD signals carry both MF and MB prediction errors (Daw et al., 2011). This undercuts a clean anatomical split. Dopamine's role goes beyond MF:
- Raising dopamine with L-DOPA increased MB weighting (Wunderlich et al., 2012).
- Dopamine neurons respond to inferred values and to **sensory prediction errors**, not only to cached rewards (Sadacca, Schoenbaum and colleagues).
- Optogenetic dopamine stimulation can drive learning of stimulus–stimulus associations.

The **orbitofrontal cortex** may supply a cognitive map of task states (Wilson, Takahashi, Schoenbaum and Niv, 2014). This would give inputs to both MB and MF computations.

MB-MF trade-offs are tied to working memory. Concurrent load (Otto et al., 2013) and acute stress shift people toward MF control. Higher working-memory capacity predicts more MB weighting.

Intermediate algorithms complicate the dichotomy:
- **The successor representation** (Dayan, 1993; Momennejad et al., 2017) caches expected future state occupancies. It adapts to reward changes but not to transition changes, which matches human revaluation data better than either pure system.
- **Dyna-style replay** uses offline simulation to train MF values. Hippocampal **sharp-wave ripple replay** has been proposed as the biological substrate (Mattar and Daw, 2018).

A further caution is that the two-step index can be contaminated by MF learners that use richer state representations. Recent analyses (Akam, Costa and Dayan, 2015) show these can mimic MB signatures. Behavioral metrics therefore need model comparison, not just stay-switch regressions.
levels.expert:
The MB/MF framework has become a backbone of **computational psychiatry**. Gillan and colleagues (2016) studied roughly 1,400 online participants and found that reduced MB control loads onto a transdiagnostic **"compulsive behavior and intrusive thought"** dimension. This dimension cuts across OCD, eating disorders and substance use disorder, and it predicted deficits better than any single diagnosis. Patients with OCD show reduced sensitivity to outcome devaluation and excessive avoidance habits (Gillan et al., 2011, 2015). Addiction is often modeled as a shift from ventral to dorsolateral striatal control (Everitt and Robbins). However, human evidence for strong habits is contested. Several careful replications failed to induce overtraining-dependent habits in healthy people (de Wit et al., 2018). Some "habits" may reflect failed goal retrieval rather than strong stimulus–response links.

Clinically relevant modulators include:
- **Parkinson's disease** (dorsolateral striatal dopamine loss) and dopaminergic therapy shift MB/MF balance.
- **Aging** reduces MB control.
- Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) disruption of dorsolateral PFC reduces MB weighting in some, but not all, studies.

The ventral capsule/ventral striatum and subthalamic nucleus, which are deep brain stimulation (DBS) targets in OCD, sit on corticostriatal loops implicated in arbitration. This makes MB/MF metrics candidate readouts of neuromodulation response, though not yet validated biomarkers.

Methodological pitfalls:
- Two-step indices have modest **test-retest reliability**, limiting individual-difference and biomarker work.
- Task variants that make MB control pay off more (Kool et al., 2016) yield more MB behavior. Measured "deficits" may therefore reflect motivation or effort costs rather than ability.
- Fitted parameters trade off with one another, for example learning rate with perseveration. Parameter recovery and model comparison should be reported.

In artificial intelligence (AI), the same tension drives hybrid agents. AlphaZero and MuZero combine learned value functions with tree search, which parallels the idea of a cached system plus a planner.

Open questions:
- How is the state space itself learned (orbitofrontal and hippocampal maps)?
- Is arbitration a discrete switch or continuous mixing?
- Do replay events during rest and sleep causally convert planning into cached values in humans?
- Can strengthening MB control, through training, stimulation or pharmacology, durably reduce compulsions?

keyPoints: Model-free learning caches action values updated by reward prediction errors
Dopamine neuron firing resembles the temporal-difference prediction error
Model-based learning plans using an internal model of transitions and rewards
Outcome devaluation separates goal-directed control from habits
Dorsomedial striatum/PFC support goal-directed control; dorsolateral striatum supports habits
Reduced model-based control is linked to compulsivity across disorders

test.q: What does a model-free learner store to guide choices?
choices: A map of how actions lead to states
test.explain: Model-free learning keeps cached action values built from experience, without a model of the task's structure.

test.q: Which signal is thought to be carried by phasic dopamine bursts?
test.explain: Dopamine neurons fire to unexpected reward and dip when expected reward is omitted, matching a prediction error.

test.q: After a food reward is devalued, which rat keeps pressing the lever?
choices: A rat with an overtrained habit
A rat given just brief training
A rat with a striatal habit lesion
test.explain: Habitual responding is insensitive to devaluation; extensive training promotes habits.

test.q: Which region is most linked to habits in rodents?
test.explain: Dorsolateral striatum supports habits; dorsomedial striatum and prelimbic cortex support goal-directed action.

test.q: A key advantage of model-based learning is that it:
choices: Ignores the structure of the task
test.explain: By planning with a model, it adjusts at once to changes like devaluation, at a higher computational cost.

test.q: In the two-step task, a rare transition is rewarded. A model-free learner tends to:
test.explain: MF simply reinforces what was just rewarded; an MB learner would switch, knowing the other option usually reaches that state.

test.q: In TD learning, the prediction error compares expected value with:
test.explain: δ = r + γV(s') − V(s): received reward plus discounted next-state value, minus current estimate.

test.q: Which factor pushes behavior toward habit?
choices: Strong contingency between action and reward
test.explain: Overtraining (and interval schedules) shifts control toward habits.

test.q: Model-based learning relies on a learned model of:
test.explain: MB learning represents which states follow actions and what each state is worth.

test.q: Making a reward unappealing to test whether behavior is goal-directed is called outcome ___.
test.explain: Outcome devaluation reveals goal-directed animals, which reduce responding.

test.q: Which neurotransmitter's neurons signal reward prediction errors?
test.explain: Midbrain dopamine neurons in VTA and substantia nigra carry prediction-error-like signals.

test.q: Automatic, model-free behaviors that persist after devaluation are called ___.
test.explain: Habits are stimulus-driven and insensitive to changes in outcome value.

kidTest.q: Walking the same way to school without thinking is a:
kidTest.explain: Doing something automatically because it worked before is a habit.

kidTest.q: What does planning use in your head?
kidTest.explain: Planning pictures a map to work out a new route.

kidTest.q: When is planning most helpful?
kidTest.explain: Planning helps when habits stop working because something changed.

kidTest.q: What is good about habits?
kidTest.explain: Habits are quick, but they can be wrong when things change.

kidTest.q: Thinking ahead with a map in your head is called p _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: Planning is the model-based way of choosing.

advancedTest.q: Under Daw, Niv and Dayan's uncertainty-based arbitration, why does overtraining produce habits?
choices: The transition model is erased by heavy repetition
Cached values grow more reliable than planned ones
Dopamine neurons stop firing after many training trials
Working memory capacity grows steadily with practice
advancedTest.explain: With lots of experience, cached MF values become low-uncertainty, so the arbitrator favors them over noisy MB computation.

advancedTest.q: A successor-representation agent experiences a change in reward location, then a change in transitions. Predicted behavior?
choices: Adapts to transitions but not rewards
Adapts to both like a full planner
Adapts to rewards but not transitions
advancedTest.explain: The SR caches future state occupancy, so reward changes are absorbed immediately but transition changes require relearning.

advancedTest.q: Why is a stay-switch regression on the two-step task alone insufficient to claim model-based control?
choices: MF learners with richer state representations can mimic MB signatures
Dopamine levels stay fixed throughout the task itself
Rare transitions occur too often for meaningful analysis
Second-stage rewards are fixed and predictable
advancedTest.explain: Akam and colleagues showed alternative MF strategies can produce apparent MB patterns, so formal model comparison is needed.

advancedTest.q: A patient group shows reduced model-based weighting on a low-payoff two-step task. The most cautious interpretation is:
choices: Their dopamine prediction errors are absent
Their dorsolateral striatum is necessarily lesioned
They have a fixed inability to form task models
Reduced effort or motivation may explain it
advancedTest.explain: MB use rises when it pays more, so low weighting can reflect cost-benefit choices rather than incapacity.

lessons.title: Theory of Mind and the Social Brain Network

levels.kid:
Have you ever guessed what a friend was thinking just by looking at their face? That clever skill is called **theory of mind**. It means knowing that other people have their own thoughts, wishes and beliefs, which can be different from yours.

Here is a famous test. Sally puts her marble in a basket and leaves. While she is gone, Anne moves it to a box. Where will Sally look? Most kids around age 4 or 5 say "the basket," because Sally didn't see the move. That means they understand Sally's mind!

Your brain has a team of helper areas for this, like a club that works together. One busy spot sits just above and behind your ears. It helps you think about what others know.
levels.hs:
**Theory of mind (ToM)** is the ability to understand that other people have mental states, such as beliefs, desires and intentions, and that these can differ from your own and from reality. The term was coined in 1978 by Premack and Woodruff, who asked whether chimpanzees have it.

The classic test is the **false-belief task**, such as the **Sally-Anne test**. A child watches Sally hide a marble in a basket. Sally leaves, and Anne moves it to a box. Asked where Sally will look, children around 4 to 5 years old usually point to the basket. They understand that Sally holds a *false belief*. Younger children often point to the box, where the marble really is.

Brain imaging shows a set of regions that become active when people think about others' minds, often called the **social brain network** or "mentalizing network":
- **Temporoparietal junction (TPJ)**, especially on the right: reasoning about what others believe
- **Medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC)**: thinking about people's traits, intentions and yourself
- **Precuneus/posterior cingulate**: imagining perspectives and scenes
- **Superior temporal sulcus (STS)**: reading eye gaze and body movement

This skill matters for friendships, cooperation and even lying or keeping secrets. Differences in theory of mind have been studied in autism, though autistic people's social understanding is more varied than a single test suggests.
levels.college:
Theory of mind (ToM), or **mentalizing**, is the attribution of mental states (beliefs, desires, intentions, knowledge) to others in order to explain and predict behavior. It is distinct from, though related to, **empathy**, which is sharing or responding to others' feelings.

**Development.** Children typically pass explicit false-belief tasks (Wimmer and Perner, 1983; Baron-Cohen, Leslie and Frith's 1985 Sally-Anne study) around age 4 to 5. Second-order beliefs ("John thinks that Mary thinks...") emerge around 6 to 7. Looking-time and anticipatory-gaze studies (Onishi and Baillargeon, 2005) suggested infants around 15 months show sensitivity to false belief, though these findings have proven hard to replicate.

**The mentalizing network.** fMRI studies comparing false-belief stories with matched "false photograph" stories (which also require representing an outdated representation, but not a mind) consistently activate:
- **Right TPJ (rTPJ)**: selective for reasoning about others' beliefs (Saxe and Kanwisher, 2003)
- **Dorsomedial PFC**: reasoning about intentions and enduring traits
- **Ventromedial PFC**: self-related and close-other judgments, linking to value
- **Precuneus/PCC**: perspective-taking and scene construction
- **Anterior temporal lobes**: social semantic knowledge, such as scripts and person knowledge
- **Posterior STS**: biological motion, gaze and action intentions

**A second system.** The **mirror/action-observation system** (ventral premotor cortex, inferior parietal lobule) responds when you perform and observe actions. It may support understanding goals of actions at a lower level, whereas the mentalizing network handles abstract beliefs. Meta-analyses (Van Overwalle and Baetens, 2009) find these two systems rarely co-activate, except when tasks demand both.

**Moral judgment.** Disrupting rTPJ with TMS makes people judge failed attempts to harm as more acceptable (Young et al., 2010). This shows intentions feed into moral evaluation.

**Clinical links.** Mentalizing differences have been described in autism, schizophrenia and frontotemporal dementia. Each has a different pattern, not a single "ToM deficit."
levels.phd:
Computationally, ToM can be framed as **inverse planning**. Observers assume agents act approximately rationally to achieve goals given their beliefs, then invert this generative model with Bayesian inference to infer hidden beliefs and desires from observed actions. Baker, Saxe and Tenenbaum's Bayesian ToM models predict human graded judgments of goals and beliefs in 2D navigation displays better than heuristic cue-based models.

**Specificity of rTPJ.** Saxe's group argued rTPJ responds selectively to the content of others' beliefs. It is not driven by mere presence of people, physical descriptions or false representations in general. Multivoxel patterns in rTPJ distinguish whether a harm was intentional or accidental (Koster-Hale et al., 2013). A competing account (Mitchell; Corbetta's attention work) notes that the TPJ is also part of the ventral attention network, which reorients attention to unexpected stimuli. Parcellation studies (Mars et al., 2012) resolved part of the dispute. They show an anterior TPJ subregion, linked to attentional reorienting, and a posterior subregion, coupled with the default network and mentalizing.

**Default mode overlap.** The mentalizing network substantially overlaps the **default mode network** (mPFC, PCC/precuneus, lateral parietal cortex, temporal poles). This supports proposals that self-projection (remembering, prospection, perspective-taking) shares core simulation machinery (Buckner and Carroll, 2007).

**Simulation vs theory theory.** Simulation accounts argue we model others by running our own mental processes "offline." Theory-theory holds that we use a folk-psychological knowledge base. Evidence supports hybrids. vmPFC activity tracks similarity between self and target (Mitchell et al., 2006), consistent with simulation for similar others and more inferential processing for dissimilar ones.

**Social learning signals.** In trust and advice-taking games, dmPFC/rTPJ encode prediction errors about others' intentions, separate from reward prediction errors (Behrens et al., 2008). Here, ACC gyrus signals tracked the volatility of a confederate's advice.

**Implicit ToM controversy.** Infant anticipatory-looking findings (Southgate et al., 2007) supported a fast, implicit "two-systems" view (Apperly and Butterfill). However, large multi-lab replication efforts (ManyBabies 2) and adult re-tests have failed to reproduce many key effects, leaving early implicit ToM unresolved.
levels.expert:
For a clinician, the social brain is often met through its failures. Frontotemporal dementia, behavioral variant (bvFTD), produces early atrophy in anterior cingulate, frontoinsula and orbitofrontal/ventromedial cortex. Patients lose empathy, tact and insight while memory and IQ tests look near-normal. Instruments such as the **Faux Pas test** and the **Reading the Mind in the Eyes Test** can detect these deficits when routine bedside cognitive screening misses them. The **von Economo neurons** of the frontoinsula and ACC are selectively lost early in bvFTD (Seeley et al.). This is one of the few cell-type links to social cognition.

**Neurosurgical relevance.**
- Resections near the right TPJ or medial prefrontal cortex can leave language and motor function intact yet impair social judgment. Standard awake-mapping tasks (naming, movement) do not test this.
- Some centers now add mentalizing tasks, such as the eyes test or false-belief vignettes, to awake mapping. Others probe subcortical white matter, including the right arcuate and cingulum, which carry the network's long-range connections.
- Studies of glioma patients report postoperative mentalizing decline that partly recovers. This suggests network-level plasticity rather than a fixed focal module.

**Pitfalls in interpretation.**
- Many ToM tasks load heavily on language, working memory and executive function. Failures in schizophrenia or after frontal injury may reflect these demands rather than a pure mentalizing deficit. Use matched control conditions.
- The "ToM deficit" account of autism is increasingly questioned. The **double empathy problem** (Milton) proposes that social mismatch runs both ways: non-autistic people are also poor at reading autistic minds. Accuracy depends on the match between perceiver and target.
- Reverse inference is a trap. TPJ or mPFC activity in a scan does not prove that mentalizing is occurring.

**Pharmacology angle.** Intranasal oxytocin was once promoted as a social-cognition enhancer. Larger trials, such as the SOARS-B trial in autistic children (2021), found no benefit on social function. Effects appear small, context-dependent and sensitive to individual differences.

**Open questions.** Can large language models that pass false-belief vignettes be said to have ToM, or do they exploit text regularities? Can network-targeted neuromodulation help? TMS over rTPJ shifts moral judgments, but therapeutic applications remain unproven.

keyPoints: Theory of mind is attributing beliefs, desires and intentions to others
False-belief tasks like Sally-Anne are typically passed around age 4-5
Right TPJ is a key hub for reasoning about others' beliefs
Mentalizing network: TPJ, mPFC, precuneus, STS, temporal poles
Mentalizing overlaps the default mode network; mirror system handles action goals
ToM deficits appear in bvFTD, and the autism 'deficit' view is debated

test.q: What does theory of mind refer to?
choices: Feeling the same emotion as another person
Recognizing familiar faces in a crowd
Remembering facts about other people's lives
Knowing others have their own beliefs
test.explain: ToM is attributing mental states to others. Sharing feelings is empathy, a related but distinct ability.

test.q: In the Sally-Anne test, a child who passes says Sally will look:
choices: In the box where the marble is now
In the basket where she left it
test.explain: Passing means recognizing Sally holds a false belief, since she did not see the marble moved.

test.q: Which region is most selectively linked to reasoning about others' beliefs?
choices: Primary visual cortex in occipital lobe
test.explain: Saxe and Kanwisher found the right TPJ responds selectively to stories about others' beliefs.

test.q: Why do fMRI studies use 'false photograph' stories as a control?
choices: They involve outdated representations but not minds
They are shorter and easier to read
They activate the visual cortex more strongly
test.explain: False photographs require tracking an outdated representation without a mind, isolating belief-specific activity.

test.q: The posterior superior temporal sulcus mainly contributes by processing:
test.explain: The pSTS responds to eye gaze, body movement and action intentions.

test.q: The mirror or action-observation system is thought to support:
choices: Understanding the goals of observed actions
test.explain: Premotor and inferior parietal mirror areas support lower-level action-goal understanding, unlike the mentalizing network.

test.q: TMS disruption of rTPJ made people judge failed attempts to harm as:
test.explain: With rTPJ disrupted, intentions weigh less, so attempted harm with no outcome seems more acceptable (Young et al., 2010).

test.q: Around what age do children usually pass second-order belief tasks?
test.explain: Second-order beliefs ('he thinks she thinks') emerge around 6 to 7, after first-order false belief at 4 to 5.

test.q: Which large-scale network overlaps substantially with the mentalizing network?
test.explain: mPFC, PCC/precuneus and lateral parietal regions are shared, suggesting common self-projection machinery.

test.q: The classic test of whether a child knows someone can hold a wrong belief is the ___-belief task.
test.explain: False-belief tasks test understanding that beliefs can differ from reality.

test.q: What abbreviation is used for the temporoparietal junction?
test.explain: TPJ is the standard abbreviation; rTPJ means right TPJ.

test.q: What is another word for theory of mind, meaning thinking about mental states?
test.explain: Mentalizing is the common synonym; the network is called the mentalizing network.

kidTest.q: What is theory of mind?
choices: Knowing others have their own thoughts
kidTest.explain: It means understanding other people think and believe their own things.

kidTest.q: Sally didn't see her marble moved. Where will she look?
kidTest.explain: She still thinks it is in the basket, because she didn't see it moved.

kidTest.q: At about what age do most kids pass the Sally test?
kidTest.explain: Most children understand Sally's mistaken belief around 4 or 5.

kidTest.q: Where is one busy brain spot for thinking about others?
kidTest.explain: The temporoparietal junction sits above and behind the ears.

kidTest.q: Guessing what a friend thinks from their f _ _ _ is part of theory of mind.
kidTest.explain: Faces give clues about what people think and feel.

advancedTest.q: Mars et al.'s TPJ parcellation helps reconcile the belief-specific and attention accounts because it shows:
choices: Attention and belief activate opposite hemispheres of the TPJ
TPJ activity is largely an artifact of eye movements in scanners
TPJ is a single area doing both jobs to an equal degree
advancedTest.explain: Distinct subregions with different connectivity let both accounts be partly right.

advancedTest.q: In inverse planning models, how is a hidden belief inferred?
choices: By inverting a model of rational goal-directed action
By reading out mirror-neuron firing directly
By counting how often an agent repeats actions
By matching faces to stored emotion templates
advancedTest.explain: Observers assume approximately rational agents and use Bayesian inference to recover beliefs and desires from actions.

advancedTest.q: A schizophrenia patient fails a long verbal false-belief vignette. The safest interpretation is:
choices: Language or working memory demands may explain it
Theory of mind is absent in schizophrenia
The rTPJ has been structurally destroyed
A pure, isolated mentalizing deficit is proven
advancedTest.explain: ToM tasks load on language and executive function, so matched controls are needed before concluding a mentalizing deficit.

advancedTest.q: vmPFC activity scaling with self-target similarity is best read as support for:
choices: Pure theory-theory for any kind of target
Using simulation more for similar others
advancedTest.explain: Mitchell et al. found similarity-dependent vmPFC engagement, consistent with self-based simulation for similar people within a hybrid account.
